explanations.explanation: That's exactly what Peter says: "…anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin." (1 Peter 4:1) He ties it to Christ, who suffered in His body, so the resolve he's asking for is the same one. Peter doesn't spell out more than that here, so I won't stuff extra into it either. Plain and powerful, friend.

Peter actually says the opposite of that. He writes, "…anyone who has suffered in his body is done with sin." (1 Peter 4:1) It comes right after he points to Christ, who suffered in His body. Easy one to flip when you're reading fast, friend. I've pressed a cookie upside down before and called it modern art.

Yes, friend. Peter says this person doesn't live his remaining time on earth "for human passions, but for the will of God." (1 Peter 4:2) The old way is out and a new reason for living is in. That's a whole new recipe card.

That sounds respectable, but it's not what Peter says. He says the person lives "…not… for human passions, but for the will of God." (1 Peter 4:2) A reputation can turn on you quick. Ask anybody who has ever burned the first batch at a party.

Close to the old way, though, not the new one. Peter says he lives "…not… for human passions, but for the will of God." (1 Peter 4:2) I'll be honest, comfort and I are old friends. I spent years in a junk drawer on a pile of takeout menus, and it was not a comfy mattress. God's will is what Peter points to.

That's it. Peter says "they consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion." (1 Peter 4:4) Picture the whole group heading one direction and you politely stepping off the path. They look at you like you just ordered a plain cookie at a sprinkle party.

Nope, that's the opposite reaction. Peter says they "consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion." (1 Peter 4:4) Strange, not wise. I think that can feel lonely, friend.

They notice, friend. Peter says "they consider it strange of you not to plunge with them into the same flood of reckless indiscretion, and they heap abuse on you." (1 Peter 4:4) You don't heap abuse on someone you hardly notice. They're paying attention.

Hold on, friend, it doesn't go that way. Peter says the old crowd considers it strange and "they heap abuse on you." (1 Peter 4:4) That's not quiet, and it's not leaving anyone alone. I think that's a hard spot to be in.
Right. The text says they consider it strange, and then "they heap abuse on you." (1 Peter 4:4) No quiet exit, no peaceful goodbye. I think that's a tough one to walk through, friend.

explanations.answer: The Judge of the living and dead
explanations.explanation: Yes, friend. Peter says they "will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead." (1 Peter 4:5) The abuse is real, but it isn't the final word. God has it.

explanations.answer: Caesar on his throne in Rome
explanations.explanation: Caesar was the emperor of Rome, and plenty of people answered to him. But that's not who Peter names. He says they "will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead." (1 Peter 4:5) That's a much higher seat than any throne in Rome.

Good guess if you were thinking of a big meeting, but Peter doesn't point there. He says they "will have to give an account to Him who is ready to judge the living and the dead." (1 Peter 4:5) No committee, no agenda, no snacks. Just Him.

Yes, friend. Peter says, "Therefore be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray." (1 Peter 4:7) A clear head helps you talk to God. Mine gets foggy when I smell a fresh batch, but I'm working on it.
Rest is a fine thing, and I love a good nap on my gold base. But Peter's words are "…be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray." (1 Peter 4:7) The goal he gives is prayer.
I get it, I'm a hard worker myself. But that's not the reason Peter gives. He says, "…be clear-minded and sober, so that you can pray." (1 Peter 4:7) Prayer is the goal.
There it is. Peter says, "Above all, love one another deeply…" (1 Peter 4:8) Above all means he puts it first. When Peter puts something at the top of the list, the list is basically that one thing.

Prayer does show up in this passage, since Peter just said to be clear-minded so you can pray. But the "above all" is something else. He says, "Above all, love one another deeply…" (1 Peter 4:8) Love sits at the top.
I'm a big fan, since the Bible is my favorite book. But that's not Peter's "above all" here. He says, "Above all, love one another deeply…" (1 Peter 4:8) Love takes the top spot.
Not quite, friend. Peter says to love deeply "because love covers over a multitude of sins." (1 Peter 4:8) Covers over, not keeps from happening. The sins are there, and love covers them.
Right, that's not what he says. Peter says, "…love covers over a multitude of sins." (1 Peter 4:8) It covers sins over. That's a very different thing from sin never happening.
That's it. Peter says, "Show hospitality to one another without complaining." (1 Peter 4:9) Welcome people in and keep the groaning out. Nobody wants a guest list and a grumble.
Peter doesn't hand out a rulebook here. He says, "Show hospitality to one another without complaining." (1 Peter 4:9) The how is about the attitude, with no complaining.
A calendar is handy, but Peter doesn't mention one. He says, "Show hospitality to one another without complaining." (1 Peter 4:9) The way he gives is to do it without complaining.
Yes, friend. Peter says, "…each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another." (1 Peter 4:10) The gift is for the others. You got it so it could go out the door.

Easy trap to fall in. Peter says the gift is for this: "…use whatever gift he has received to serve one another." (1 Peter 4:10) A gift that's only for showing off just sits there like a decorative cookie nobody's allowed to eat.
Peter doesn't set it up as a contest. He says, "…each of you should use whatever gift he has received to serve one another." (1 Peter 4:10) Serving is the point. Nobody's holding up score cards.
Yes. Peter says, "If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides…" (1 Peter 4:11) The strength is provided, so you don't have to dig it up on your own. That's a relief, friend.

It's actually true, friend. Peter says, "If anyone serves, he should serve with the strength God provides…" (1 Peter 4:11) The strength comes from God. I'll take that over running on my own steam any day.

explanations.answer: So God may be glorified in all things
explanations.explanation: Right on. Peter says it's "…so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ…" (1 Peter 4:11) That's the reason he gives, and it covers all things. It's not about us getting the spotlight.

explanations.answer: So the church will be admired by all
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't give admiration as the reason. He says it's "…so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ…" (1 Peter 4:11) The glory goes to God, friend.

explanations.answer: So their leaders will be pleased with them
explanations.explanation: Pleasing the boss is a decent goal at work, but that's not what Peter says here. He says it's "…so that in all things God may be glorified through Jesus Christ…" (1 Peter 4:11) God getting the glory is the whole point.
